basic_info.competition_series: FSG (Formula Student Germany) - primary; also FS Italy (FSI), and since 2026 FS Switzerland (Driverless Cup) and FS Czech
basic_info.summary: AMZ (Akademischer Motorsportverein Zürich), founded 2006, moved from combustion to electric racecars in 2010 and became the pioneer of the Formula Student Driverless (FSD) discipline when it launched in 2017. Their car flüela driverless won the inaugural FSG Driverless event at Hockenheim on 13 August 2017, the only team of 15 entrants to finish every discipline, and the follow-on car gotthard driverless won FS Italy and FSG again in 2018, beating numerous lap-time records. AMZ's open-sourced fsd_skeleton ROS architecture and its 2019 arXiv/JFR paper 'AMZ Driverless: The Full Autonomous Racing System' became the de facto reference architecture copied by dozens of later FSD teams worldwide. The program is built on top of AMZ's existing, highly optimized 4WD electric racecar platform (0-100km/h in 1.9s) rather than a from-scratch chassis, and used dual-redundant LiDAR/camera perception, FastSLAM 2.0 mapping, and nonlinear MPC control. AMZ continues to compete at the front of the DV field through 2026 (car 'nera').

history.ramp_phases: [uncertain] No explicitly named ramp phases were found in AMZ's own sources. Inferred from the system paper's structure: (1) architecture design & sim tooling stand-up (FSSIM on Gazebo, ATS regression harness), (2) sensor/actuator bring-up on the existing EV chassis (EBS, steering motor, dual compute), (3) SLAM-mode track mapping with pure-pursuit for lap 1, (4) localization-mode MPC racing once a map exists, (5) post-season iteration/refinement for the following year's car.
history.what_slipped: The system paper explicitly identifies end-to-end pipeline latency (~300ms cone-detection-to-control-command, 500ms for the vision pipeline specifically) as 'one of the biggest bottlenecks in our current architecture,' forcing the team to cap top speed and wheel torque below what the hardware could otherwise achieve - i.e., software/latency maturity lagged the mechanical/electrical platform's capability and became the limiting factor rather than a discrete schedule slip.
history.platform_prerequisites: Yes. AMZ did not build a dedicated DV chassis; it retrofitted its existing, already race-proven 4WD electric racecar (190 kg, 0-100km/h in 1.9s, full aero package, custom tires) with an EBS, steering motor, sensors, and dual onboard computers. The EV platform itself had been under continuous development since AMZ's 2010 shift to electric racing, giving the DV program a mature base rather than requiring its own EV conversion.

technical_features.ebs_design: Emergency Braking System (EBS) mounted behind the brake pedals; can only either fully apply or fully release the mechanical (hydraulic) brakes - it is a binary emergency actuator, not a proportional one, and is not used for normal autonomous driving (which decelerates via motor regeneration instead). Per the related ICRA 2018 paper (de la Iglesia Valls et al.), the safety concept comprises two fully independent pneumatic and hydraulic circuits for the front and rear brake circuits, with pressurized air from onboard tanks driving pneumatic cylinders that independently press the brake master cylinders. Can be triggered either from the Remote Emergency System (RES) or from onboard fault detection, satisfying DT.3.2/DT.3.3.
technical_features.ebs_development_duration: [uncertain] Not disclosed numerically in accessible sources
technical_features.steering_actuation: A motor was added under the front axle as the steering actuator, capable of moving from full lock left to full lock right in under 0.9s. Manual steering rack is retained so the car can be steered manually when the DSMS is off (DT.2.1.1); specific decoupling mechanism per DT.2.2 not detailed in accessible sources. [uncertain: exact motor model/gearing not disclosed]
technical_features.brake_actuation: For normal autonomous driving (non-emergency), deceleration is generated purely by regenerative braking through the 4 hub-mounted drive motors - the mechanical service brakes are not actively used except by the EBS in an emergency. This is a distinctive design choice compared with teams that use a separate powered service-brake actuator.
technical_features.sensor_mounting_packaging: 3D LiDAR mounted on the front wing (maximizes point returns per cone and unobstructed forward FoV). Three CMOS global-shutter cameras (2 stereo, 1 mono) mounted on the main roll hoop above the driver's seat in a self-developed housing, minimizing cone-to-cone occlusion. INS/IMU and GNSS antennas mounted per Fig. 4 of the system paper; dual antenna setup for accurate heading.
technical_features.mass_added: [uncertain] Total vehicle mass with DV system is 190 kg (per Kabzan et al. 2019) / 181 kg (per Advanced Navigation case study, likely a different model year) - sources disagree slightly and neither isolates the DV-system-only mass delta.
technical_features.chassis_impact: Self-developed camera and compute housings were engineered as bespoke mounts (Fig. 3 of the system paper) rather than off-the-shelf enclosures; LiDAR mount integrated into the front wing structure. No further chassis/suspension/aero redesign details found in accessible sources.
technical_features.compute_platform: Two onboard computers: a rugged industrial 'master' PC (with an NVIDIA GTX 1050Ti GPU) running SLAM, boundary estimation, and control, and an embedded NVIDIA Jetson TX2 'slave' running the LiDAR/vision perception nodes and velocity estimation - architected so the car can still race if the slave fails (only non-critical pipeline parts run there). A separate low-level ECU (PIP39) interfaces directly with actuators and performs safety checks/low-level control, independent of the two main computers.
technical_features.sensor_suite: 3D LiDAR (front wing mounted, model not specified in accessible sources); 3x CMOS global-shutter cameras (2 stereo, 5.5mm focal length/64.5° HFOV lenses for close cones; 1 mono, 12mm focal length/54.5° HFOV for cones at 7-15m); dual-antenna Inertial Navigation System (Advanced Navigation Spatial Dual) providing IMU + 0.08° heading accuracy; industrial-grade laser-based non-contact optical Ground Speed Sensor (GSS); steering-angle encoder in the steering rack; 4x wheel hub motor resolvers (angular speed); motor-controller torque feedback per wheel.
technical_features.shutdown_circuit_implementation: [uncertain] Not detailed with specific relay wiring in accessible sources beyond the general architecture (ECU handles safety checks and can trigger the EBS); rule references DT.4.1-DT.4.3 (DS relay, Remote Stop relay, EBS relay) apply but no team-specific implementation detail was found.
technical_features.remote_stop_system: Remote Emergency System (RES) can trigger the EBS; specific vendor/model not disclosed in accessible sources. [uncertain]
technical_features.status_indicators: [uncertain] Not detailed in accessible sources (DSSI/DT.1.3 implementation specifics not found)
technical_features.custom_pcbs: Self-developed camera housing and computing-system housing (Fig. 3a/3b of the system paper) integrating an industrial Ethernet switch, GPU cooling, and Jetson TX2 mounting; development duration/cost not disclosed. [uncertain on duration]
technical_features.software_stack: ROS-based, split across three execution domains: perception (LiDAR + vision nodes) on the Jetson TX2 'slave'; SLAM, boundary estimation, and MPC control on the industrial 'master' PC; low-level control and safety checks on the dedicated ECU. The publicly released fsd_skeleton reference repository organizes code into 0_fsd_common, 1_perception (lidar/visual cone detection), 2_estimation (velocity estimator, SLAM), and 3_control packages - this structure became the template many other FSD teams copied.
technical_features.ros_version: ROS Kinetic on Ubuntu 16.04 (per the public fsd_skeleton reference repository; the specific distro used on the 2017/2018 competition cars themselves was not explicitly confirmed in accessible sources). [uncertain: exact distro on the real competition car vs. the published skeleton]
technical_features.perception_approach: Dual independent, redundant pipelines. LiDAR pipeline: FoV trimming -> adaptive ground-plane removal (regression per angular/radial bin) -> Euclidean clustering -> cylindrical cluster reconstruction -> rule-based cluster legality filter -> CNN-based color classification (4 conv + 5 FC layers, 32x32 grayscale intensity image input, reliable color ID out to 4.5m). Camera pipeline: modified YOLOv2 multi-object detector -> keypoint regression (ResNet-based CNN, Dhall et al. 2019) -> monocular PnP+RANSAC pose estimation for far cones (7-15m) or stereo SIFT-feature triangulation for close cones; vision distance error <1.0m at 15m from the car. Fusion/cross-validation between the two pipelines gives robustness to single-sensor failure.
technical_features.slam_localization_approach: FastSLAM 2.0 (particle-filter SLAM, chosen over EKF-SLAM for linear-in-landmarks scaling and multi-hypothesis data association) builds a map of colored cone landmarks during the first ('SLAM mode') lap at 15Hz mapping / 200Hz odometry-propagation localizer rate; lap-closure is detected via particle-spread, heading-match, and proximity-to-start heuristics, after which the system switches to 'Localization mode' using Monte Carlo Localization against the frozen best-particle map. Landmark color is tracked via Dirichlet-conjugate Bayesian updates per landmark. Separately, a 9-state Extended Kalman Filter (position/velocity/acceleration/slip-ratio) fuses 6 sensor sources (GSS, IMU, GNSS, WSS, motor torque, steering angle) for velocity estimation, with chi-square outlier rejection plus a variance-based drift detector for sensor-failure handling. Validated to RMSE ~0.2-0.25m against Leica Totalstation ground truth.
technical_features.planning_approach: Delaunay triangulation (via CGAL library) discretizes the cone observations into a graph; a breadth-first, beam-search-pruned tree of candidate center-line paths is grown through the triangulation in a receding-horizon fashion (re-planned every 50ms, sensor range ~10m); a 5-term cost function (max angle change, track-width std-dev, cone-spacing std-dev, color-probability mismatch penalty, path-length-vs-sensor-range) picks the most likely track center line/boundary. The resulting path is followed with a pure pursuit controller for the mapping lap.
technical_features.control_approach: For 'Localization mode' laps (once the track is mapped), a real-time nonlinear Model Predictive Contouring Control (MPC) formulation directly maximizes progress along the reference spline subject to the vehicle's dynamics and track/tire limits. Vehicle model blends a dynamic bicycle model (simplified Pacejka tire model) with a kinematic bicycle model for low-speed validity, plus input-rate dynamics and a friction-ellipse tire constraint. Solved as a 10-state/3-input nonlinear program via the commercial ForcesPro NLP solver at 50ms sampling, 40-step (2s) horizon; 90% of solves complete under the 50ms cycle time (worst case 65ms).
technical_features.simulation_tooling: FSSIM - AMZ's own open-sourced simulator, built on the Gazebo simulation framework but replacing Gazebo's physics engine with an integrated first-principles vehicle model matched to real vehicle performance; the track surface is a flat plane with constant friction, auto-generated from log data; perception sensors are not simulated (too computationally expensive) - instead, cone observations with configurable noise models are injected directly. Runs automatically on every pull request into the main branch plus nightly regression runs.
technical_features.ci_cd_testing: 'Automated Testing System' (ATS): a distributed, PostgreSQL-backed job-queue architecture with polling worker nodes for (a) simulation and (b) log visualization; triggered by CI (PRs) and nightly on the main branch; failures generate notifications; results (pass/fail, lap-time stats) are surfaced through a web dashboard with automated RViz-based visualizations of every log.
technical_features.data_logging: rosbag format (ROS-standard), the entire data pipeline (recording, archiving, indexing, browsing, and automated visualization) is built around it and surfaced through ATS's web interface.
technical_features.open_source_repos: github.com/AMZ-Driverless: fsd_skeleton - the publicly released reference ROS architecture (dummy nodes across perception/estimation/control) that became the canonical starting-point template copied by numerous later FSD teams; fssim - the open-source Gazebo-based simulator; fsd-resources - supplementary learning resources; rbb_core - the data-logging/ATS framework. These repos are widely cited/forked and are arguably AMZ's single most influential contribution to the broader FSD community.

milestone_significance.critical_path_items: 1) Building genuine sensor/pipeline redundancy (fully independent LiDAR and camera perception paths, plus multi-sensor EKF with explicit failure detection) so that no single sensor failure could end a run - repeatedly cited as a 'confirmed need' after failures were observed 'throughout the testing seasons.' 2) SLAM/localization accuracy sufficient to handle cone spacing as tight as the rules allow while operating within a limited (~10m) perception horizon. 3) End-to-end system latency (~300-500ms sensor-to-actuator), which the team itself names as 'one of the biggest bottlenecks' constraining how fast the car could safely be driven, ultimately capping top speed and torque below the platform's mechanical capability.
milestone_significance.long_lead_procurement: [uncertain] No numeric lead times (in weeks) were disclosed in accessible sources for the LiDAR, Advanced Navigation Spatial Dual INS, or Jetson TX2/industrial compute hardware.
milestone_significance.first_dynamic_test_date: [uncertain] Not disclosed precisely; inferred to be prior to the 13 Aug 2017 FSG debut, likely mid-2017
milestone_significance.validation_strategy: Combination of (1) nightly/PR-triggered automated simulation regression via ATS/FSSIM to catch problems before real-world testing, (2) real-world track testing explicitly designed to 'push the car to the limit' - aggressive driving, challenging track layouts, and adverse weather - rather than only nominal conditions, (3) deliberate sensor-failure injection testing to validate the chi-square + variance-based drift detectors in the EKF, and (4) ground-truth surveying (Leica Totalstation) to quantify SLAM/localization RMSE against independently measured cone positions and car trajectory.

competition_ecosystem.rules_compliance_challenges: [uncertain] Not detailed with specifics in accessible sources; general redundancy requirements under the DT rule set (dual independent perception pipelines, dual/triple sensing for velocity estimation) appear to have driven much of the architecture, consistent with meeting DT.3/DT.4 safety-relay and shutdown-circuit requirements, but no first-person account of specific rule difficulties was found.

performance_metrics.dv_event_results: FSG 2017: 1st overall (only team of 15 to finish all disciplines), fastest lap 55.53s, total time 557.89s. FS Italy 2018: 1st overall, total 776.28s. FSG 2018: 1st overall, fastest lap 28.48s, total 285.93s, 'beating numerous score records'; consistent 10-lap Trackdrive times ranging 28.483s-28.913s. FS Switzerland 2026: 1st place Driverless Cup with a perfect 600/600 points (car 'nera'). FS Czech 2026: 2nd Driverless Cup. FSG 2026: 3rd Driverless Cup.
performance_metrics.autonomous_speeds_achieved: Up to 1.5g lateral acceleration (14.7 m/s^2) measured over ten competition laps at FSG 2018; typical racing speeds up to roughly 15 m/s per the GG-plot velocity color scale in the system paper.
performance_metrics.ebs_deceleration_achieved: [uncertain] Not disclosed numerically in accessible sources
performance_metrics.perception_range_achieved: LiDAR-camera color classification reliable out to 4.5m (limited by point-cloud sparsity beyond that range); vision-pipeline distance error stays under 1.0m at 15m from the car; overall path-planning cost function is tuned around a ~10m effective sensor range.
performance_metrics.reliability_notes: AMZ was the only team of 15 entrants to finish every discipline at the first-ever FSD event (FSG 2017). Sensor failures (both outlier spikes and sustained drift, e.g. GNSS dropouts) were observed 'throughout the testing seasons,' motivating the dual chi-square/variance-based failure-detection scheme in the EKF; no major on-track reliability failures are reported in the winning runs described in the paper.

top_mistakes: From the paper's own 'Lessons Learned' section: the team stresses that only real-world testing, not simulation alone, can thoroughly evaluate the whole system - implying that early reliance on subsystem-level testing without regular full-pipeline integration testing was a risk they had to correct for ('the full pipeline should still be tested regularly to verify it works as a whole and that overall computational constraints are met'). They also flag that fixed, cleanly separated subsystem interfaces (good for parallel development) can mask integration-level problems if not deliberately re-tested together.
advice_for_new_teams: Paraphrased from the system paper's conclusion/lessons section: (1) 'hardware is important, and only real-world testing can thoroughly evaluate the whole system' - keep development/testing cycles short so features can be evaluated in time for competition; (2) invest in simulation specifically to make real-world testing more efficient, not as a replacement for it; (3) when testing, deliberately push to extreme cases - aggressive driving, challenging track layouts, and both good and poor weather - to 'better understand the car' and 'successfully compete... where it is key to go to the limit but not beyond'; (4) build a safety calculator to compute required test-track clearance distances from max speed, human reaction time, and communication delay before testing near people or obstacles.
team_structure_dv: [uncertain] The 2019 system paper lists 20 named co-authors (from AMZ Driverless plus ETH's Autonomous Systems Lab and Automatic Control Laboratory). One unverified web summary suggested a build team of '18 students' and a broader active membership of 'approximately 35 people' backed by alumni, but these figures could not be confirmed against a primary source and are flagged uncertain.

recommended_sequence: Inferred from AMZ's own build order and stated priorities: (1) secure/retain a proven, well-instrumented EV racecar platform rather than building a DV-specific chassis; (2) add EBS + steering actuator + minimal redundant sensing early, reusing regenerative braking for normal autonomous deceleration instead of building a new service-brake actuator; (3) build a robust multi-sensor EKF velocity/state estimator (using sensors already needed for the EV car) before tackling perception; (4) build FastSLAM-based mapping plus a simple pure-pursuit controller to reliably complete a first mapping lap; (5) layer path-planning cost-function refinement on top of the Delaunay/graph-search structure; (6) only add MPC control once mapping/localization is trustworthy and a validated vehicle model exists; (7) build an automated simulation/regression testing harness (their ATS) in parallel from early on, but never let it substitute for full-pipeline, real-world, edge-case testing; (8) validate EBS and sensor redundancy specifically under deliberately induced failure conditions before the first competition.
applicability_to_24_month_ramp: AMZ's own history shows that a strong existing EV racecar plus a focused software effort can produce a winning DV entry within roughly a single build season (an estimated 12-18 months from architecture kickoff to a first-time competition win) - a 24-month (June 2026-June 2028) window gives a comparable team meaningfully more runway than AMZ had for its first car. Highest-value transferable practices for a ~9-person, software-focused team: (1) invest early in an automated simulation/regression harness (AMZ's ATS) rather than relying solely on scarce track time, since AMZ explicitly credits this with making real-world testing more efficient; (2) build sensor redundancy (independent LiDAR and camera pipelines, multi-sensor EKF with explicit failure detection) into the architecture from day one rather than retrofitting it after failures are observed in testing, since AMZ found the need for redundancy 'confirmed... throughout the testing seasons'; (3) sequence software complexity the way AMZ did - FastSLAM/pure-pursuit for a 'good enough' first lap, MPC only once mapping/localization is proven - to avoid over-investing early effort in the hardest control problem; (4) treat total system latency (AMZ's own self-identified bottleneck at ~300-500ms) as a first-class, continuously measured design metric rather than an afterthought, since it directly capped their competitive top speed even after winning.
